concepts.explain: In lj units every quantity is dimensionless: distances are multiples of sigma, energies multiples of epsilon. Nothing is in angstroms or kcal/mol.
Every atom carries a numeric type. Force field parameters are assigned per type, not per atom, so type is what decides how an atom behaves.
A region is a named shape in space. The simulation box is built from a region, and only then can atoms exist.
An integer that fixes the random sequence. The same seed reproduces the same run exactly; change it for a statistically independent repeat.
Beyond the cutoff the pair interaction is simply not computed. Too short clips the attractive well; too long spends compute on forces near zero.
Parameters for unlike pairs are derived from the like pairs, by default as geometric means. You rarely need to write them out yourself.
Every fix reads the same way: an ID you choose, the group it acts on, then the style and its arguments.
The integrator advances time in discrete jumps. Each jump must be short compared with the fastest motion, or the integration goes unstable.
LAMMPS prints a line of thermodynamic data every so many steps, and the GUI charts whatever columns you ask for.

steps.title: The five sections of an input script
steps.teach:
A LAMMPS script is read strictly top to bottom, and the order matters: some commands only work *before* the simulation box exists, others only after. Rather than memorize that, the script is laid out in five labelled sections and filled in turn.

Your editor already holds them as comments. Everything after a `#` is ignored by LAMMPS.

We start with **Initialization**: what units to work in, how many dimensions, what an atom is, and what happens at the edges of the box.

commands.explain: Work in reduced units, where the Lennard-Jones parameters are defined as 1.

notes.alternatives: `real` gives angstroms and kcal/mol; `metal` gives angstroms and eV. Changing this changes the meaning of every number below it.

commands.explain: Simulate in 3D. In 2D the atoms are confined to the xy-plane.

notes.alternatives: `2` confines atoms to the xy-plane, which is a common trick for cheap visual demonstrations.

commands.explain: The simplest kind of particle: a point with a mass and a type, nothing else.

notes.alternatives: `charge` adds a per-atom charge, `molecular` adds bonds and molecule IDs. Pick the cheapest style that holds what you need.

commands.explain: Periodic in all three directions: an atom leaving one face re-enters through the opposite one.

notes.alternatives: `f` is a fixed wall, `s` shrink-wraps to the atoms, `m` shrink-wraps with a minimum. A slab would use `p p f`.

steps.title: A box, and atoms in it
steps.teach:
Now the **System definition** section. A *region* is only a shape; the simulation box is built from it, and only then can atoms exist.

This tutorial simulates a binary mixture: 1500 small atoms of type 1 and 100 larger ones of type 2, dropped in at random.

commands.explain: Define a cube 40 units on a side, centred on the origin, named simbox.

notes.note: the name you will refer to it by
notes.alternatives: Any name works; you use it again in the next command.
`sphere`, `cylinder` and `prism` are also available, and regions can be combined with union and intersect.

notes.note: the six bounds, as xlo xhi ylo yhi zlo zhi
notes.alternatives: Making the box smaller at fixed atom count raises the density, which you will do later.

commands.explain: Build the box from that region, with room for two atom types.

notes.note: how many atom types will exist
notes.alternatives: This is locked in from here on. Referring to a type 3 later would be an error, and every type declared needs a mass and pair parameters.

commands.explain: Drop 1500 atoms of type 1 into the box at random positions.

notes.alternatives: More atoms means better statistics and a slower run.
Change it for a different arrangement of the same system.

Without it, two atoms can land almost on top of each other. The Lennard-Jones repulsion goes as 1/r^12, so that produces an enormous force -- exactly the instability you will trigger on purpose later.

commands.explain: Add 100 atoms of the second, heavier type. A different seed gives a different arrangement.

steps.title: Masses and how atoms feel each other
steps.teach:
The **Settings** section. Nothing can be computed until every atom type has a mass and every pair of types knows how to interact.

The Lennard-Jones potential is `4*eps*[(sig/r)^12 - (sig/r)^6]`. The 12 term is the hard repulsion at close range; the 6 term is the weak long-range attraction that lets a fluid condense instead of dispersing.

commands.explain: Atom type 1 is the light species.
Type 2 is five times heavier, so at the same temperature it moves more sluggishly.
All pairs interact through a truncated Lennard-Jones potential.

notes.alternatives: `lj/cut/coul/long` adds long-range electrostatics; `eam` is for metals. This one line decides the physics.
2.5 is the more common convention in the literature; this tutorial keeps more of the attractive tail at 4.0.

commands.explain: Epsilon and sigma for a type 1 atom meeting another type 1 atom.

notes.note: epsilon, the depth of the potential well
notes.alternatives: Larger epsilon means a stronger attraction and a fluid that condenses more readily.

notes.note: sigma, the distance where the energy crosses zero
notes.alternatives: Roughly the atom's diameter. There is no default for either value: lj/cut requires both.

commands.explain: The heavy species: a shallower well but a much larger diameter.

notes.alternatives: You never write a 1-2 line. LAMMPS mixes it: eps_12 = sqrt(1.0 x 0.5) = 0.707, sigma_12 = sqrt(1.0 x 3.0) = 1.732. `pair_modify` chooses a different rule.

steps.title: Ask for output, then relax the structure
steps.teach:
The **Monitoring** and **Run** sections.

The atoms were placed at random, so some pairs sit far closer than sigma and the potential energy starts large and *positive*. Minimization slides them downhill into a nearby local minimum before any dynamics begin.

figure.caption: Your system before minimization -- atoms placed at random.

commands.explain: Print a line of thermodynamic data every 10 steps.

notes.alternatives: Larger values print less and run marginally faster. This run is short, so keep it frequent.

commands.explain: Report the step number, the total energy, and the pressure.

notes.alternatives: `temp`, `pe` and `ke` are the other common ones. Whatever you list here is what the Charts window can plot.

commands.explain: Slide the atoms downhill until one of four stopping criteria is met.

notes.note: energy tolerance, then force tolerance, then iteration and evaluation limits
notes.alternatives: Minimization finds a *local* minimum, never the global one. That is fine here: the point is only to remove the bad contacts.

steps.title: Integrate the equations of motion
steps.teach:
Nothing moves in LAMMPS unless a *fix* makes it move. `fix nve` integrates Newton's equations with the velocity-Verlet algorithm and adds nothing else -- no thermostat, no barostat.

With periodic boundaries and no thermostat, this samples the microcanonical (NVE) ensemble: constant number of particles, volume and energy.

commands.explain: Report less often now: this run is much longer than the minimization.

commands.text: thermo_style custom step temp etotal pe ke press
commands.explain: Once the atoms move there is a temperature and a kinetic energy worth watching, and pe + ke = etotal.
Integrate every atom's motion, every step.

notes.note: an ID you choose, used later to modify or delete this fix

notes.alternatives: `all` is a default group containing every atom. You can define your own groups to thermostat only part of a system.
`nvt` would add a thermostat and hold temperature instead of energy; `npt` would also control pressure.

commands.explain: Advance time in steps of 0.005 reduced time units.

notes.note: how far time moves each step
notes.alternatives: This is the number you are about to break on purpose.

commands.explain: 125 reduced time units of dynamics. The system starts far from equilibrium: potential energy falls while kinetic energy climbs, until both plateau.

notes.alternatives: Longer runs give better statistics. Everything here is deliberately short enough to finish on a laptop.

steps.title: Push the timestep until it fails
steps.teach:
Every MD practitioner meets this failure, usually at the worst possible moment. Far better to meet it here, in a system you can reset in seconds.

Raise the timestep and re-run. Somewhere above about 0.02 the integrator can no longer track the fastest collisions: it steps an atom straight through its neighbour's repulsive core, the atom comes out with an enormous velocity, and the total energy climbs without bound.

If the run stops with **ERROR: Lost atoms**, that is what happened. It almost never means atoms were really lost -- it means the integration went unstable, and the timestep is the first thing to check.

params.label: timestep
params.explain: Start where you are, then push it up in stages and re-run each time. Watch the total energy column rather than waiting for an error.

prediction.question: Before you run it -- what will the total energy do at a timestep of 0.05?

options.feedback: It does in exact arithmetic, and with a good timestep it very nearly does in practice. But conservation is a property of the *equations*, not of the approximation used to integrate them.
Right. Energy is created out of nothing because the integrator is no longer solving the equations of motion -- it is generating noise.
Energy is not being drained anywhere: there is no thermostat and no friction in this script. The failure mode is runaway, not decay.

steps.expect: the total energy trace in the Charts window, and whether the run survives to the end

steps.title: Put it back, and notice what LAMMPS never told you
steps.teach:
Set the timestep back to something stable and confirm the system behaves again.

Note what LAMMPS did **not** do: it accepted `timestep 0.05` without a word of complaint, because that is perfectly valid syntax. No error message told you the value was wrong. Only the physics did -- which is why watching the energy trace is not optional.

params.label: timestep
params.explain: 0.005 is where this tutorial started, and it is a conventional choice for Lennard-Jones in reduced units.

steps.expect: a total energy that fluctuates around a constant value instead of climbing

steps.title: Choose a temperature instead of accepting one
steps.teach:
So far the temperature has been whatever the system happened to settle at -- nobody chose it. A Langevin thermostat adds friction and a random kick to every atom; the two balance at a target temperature, and the ensemble becomes canonical (NVT) rather than microcanonical.

Insert the thermostat first if it is not in your script yet, then try different target temperatures.

commands.explain: Hold the temperature at 1.0 throughout the run.

notes.note: target temperature at the start of the run
notes.alternatives: Making the start and end values differ ramps the temperature over the run, which is how you heat or quench a system.
Smaller values couple the thermostat more strongly and disturb the dynamics more; larger values equilibrate more slowly.

params.label: target temperature
params.explain: Low temperatures let the attraction dominate and the fluid condenses; high temperatures push it towards a gas. Watch the snapshot as well as the chart.

steps.expect: how the structure changes between a cold and a hot run -- and how long the temperature takes to settle

steps.title: Change the mixture itself
steps.teach:
Two last things worth trying, both one number each.

Make the heavy species attract itself strongly and see whether the two components separate. Or change how many large atoms there are and watch the structure change.

Nothing here is graded, and the script is yours now.

params.label: epsilon for the heavy pair
params.explain: Raising this makes large atoms stick to each other. Past about 2.0 they tend to cluster together rather than mix.

steps.expect: whether the heavy atoms stay dispersed or clump into a separate phase
